question: A facilities manager wants Claude to turn her site-visit notes into short summaries that engineers read on their phones between jobs, so each summary must stay under 150 words. She will make this same request many times with different notes. How should she express the length limit?
options: A) Ask for the shortest summary she can get, and then cut anything back that still runs over the word limit.
B) State the 150-word limit and the reason for it: engineers read the summaries on a phone between jobs.
C) State the 150-word limit on its own, as any explanation around it only lengthens her request.
D) Repeat the 150-word limit in capital letters at the start and again at the end of the request.
correct_answers: B) State the 150-word limit and the reason for it: engineers read the summaries on a phone between jobs.
explanations: An unspecified target produces inconsistent lengths and moves the work back onto the manager.
Correct. Giving the reason behind a constraint lets Claude apply the underlying intent sensibly to new notes, rather than treating 150 words as an arbitrary rule to satisfy.
The limit alone works, but without the reason Claude cannot judge what to keep when notes vary.
Emphasis and repetition do not add information; the constraint was already clear the first time.
